AI agents are getting f...cking good at building other AI agents

10 GitHub repos for turning GPT 6 Astra into an AI engineering lab that generates training data, improves models, and tests what actually works

01 DSPy  
▸ https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy  
→ optimize prompts and AI pipelines programmatically

GENERATE THE TRAINING DATA

02 Distilabel  
▸ https://github.com/argilla-io/distilabel  
→ generate and process synthetic datasets with LLMs

03 DataDreamer  
▸ https://github.com/datadreamer-dev/DataDreamer  
→ build reproducible synthetic data workflows

04 Argilla  
▸ https://github.com/argilla-io/argilla  
→ collect human feedback and curate datasets

TRAIN THE SPECIALISTS

05 Unsloth  
▸ https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth  
→ accelerate fine tuning with optimized training workflows

06 LLaMA Factory  
▸ https://github.com/hiyouga/LLaMA-Factory  
→ fine tune and evaluate open models

07 Axolotl  
▸ https://github.com/axolotl-ai-cloud/axolotl  
→ configure and run model training pipelines

TEST WHAT ACTUALLY IMPROVED

08 lm-evaluation-harness  
▸ https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness  
→ benchmark models across standardized tasks

09 OpenCompass  
▸ https://github.com/open-compass/opencompass  
→ evaluate model capabilities across multiple benchmarks

DEPLOY THE WINNERS

10 BentoML  
▸ https://github.com/bentoml/BentoML  
→ package and serve models as production services

the architecture:

GPT 6 Astra → generate data → curate → fine tune → benchmark → compare → deploy → collect feedback → repeat

3 builds worth bookmarking:

coding specialist: DSPy → Distilabel → Unsloth → lm-evaluation-harness

research specialist: DataDreamer → Argilla → LLaMA Factory → OpenCompass

production lab: Distilabel → Axolotl → lm-evaluation-harness → BentoML

here's the part most people miss

you don't need your most powerful model answering every question

you can use it to help create the data and workflows that make smaller models useful for specific jobs

one powerful model helping build an entire fleet of specialists

that's a much more interesting use of intelligence ⭣

article.title: Build Your Own AI Employees on GPT-6 Astra: The A–Z Agent Playbook

blocks.text: The to-do list on your laptop is honest. It moves when you sit down. It freezes when you stand up.
You know the morning. Inbox first. Three forms that were “quick” last Tuesday. A person you have chased twice who still has not sent the file.
You answer, you nudge, you fill, you paste the same paragraph into a new window. By noon the list looks like last night, only heavier.
That is not a willpower problem. That is a company with one employee, and the employee is you.
I used to treat GPT-6 Astra like a very fast colleague in a chat box. I sat with it. I steered it.
The work advanced in the minutes I was looking. The minute I left, the company clocked out.
GPT-6 Astra was still fast. The company was still me.
Then I hired the work into homemade agents and put GPT-6 Astra underneath them as the engine. One agent owned triage. One owned the form pack. One waited for a handoff, then wrote the chase notes.
I shut the lid. When I opened it, the result was not a wall of chat. It was a dated folder: a one-page brief, a draft pack, and an action log of who had been pinged and who still needed a human.
GPT-6 Astra is the engine. Your homemade agents are the employees.
This is the A–Z playbook for standing up that roster on a laptop, a VPS, or a cloud computer you actually control.
Seven steps. Stop after the first and you still have a hire. Run all seven and the week can move when you are not in the chair.
Hire one agent and shut the lid.
Write the charter, then leave it alone.
Give tools and logins once.
Put GPT-6 Astra behind every agent.
Hire the rest by what they own.
Make agents hand work to each other.
Put the roster on a schedule.
Step 1 · Hire one agent and shut the lid
Start with one body of work that already has a finish line. Not “help me with ops.” A job you could hand a careful intern on a Friday and check on Monday.
The first hire is Owen, in miniature. Weekly ops: the unanswered inbound, the form that is always almost done, the person who was supposed to send the file.
Give the agent a name, a folder, and a definition of done that lives on disk.

Name: Owen. Owns: the weekly residue pack. Done: a dated folder with three artifacts. A one-page brief of what arrived. A draft of the recurring form, unsubmitted. An action log of chases written, not sent.
That last clause matters. The first agent does not get to touch the outside world. It prepares. You still press send, submit, and pay.
Run the job once while you watch. You need the shape of a good finish before you trust a closed lid.
Judge the run by the folder, not the chat. If the brief, the draft, and the log are there, the hire worked.
If the chat is brilliant and the folder is empty, the hire failed. A transcript is not a shift. A folder is.
The second run is the real interview. Same job. Same folder pattern.
This time you shut the lid. Go make coffee. Come back to the artifact, not to a conversation that needs you to keep it alive.

A homemade agent is not a prompt you retype. It is a small runtime on your machine: a role file, a workspace, permission to use a browser and a filesystem, and an instruction to stop when the artifacts exist.
GPT-6 Astra is what thinks inside that loop. The agent is the employee who was told what “done” looks like.
GPT-6 Astra is not the intern. The intern is the agent you named and left.
Keep the first job boring on purpose. Boring is measurable. “Summarize my life” is not, and “build me a company” is not.
“Put last week’s inbound into ops/2026-09-14/ with a brief, a draft, and a log” is a job an employee can finish without you.
Three tests before you promote this agent.
The lid test. You left. The folder still appeared.
The stranger test. Someone who is not you can open the folder and know what happened.
The repeat test. Tuesday’s pack looks like Monday’s pack, same bones, new facts.
Lid. Stranger. Repeat.
Fail the lid test and you still have a chatbot. Fail the stranger test and you still have a diary. Fail the repeat test and you still have a one-off.
GPT-6 Astra can pass a chat. Only the folder proves an employee.
Pass all three, and you have an employee. Do not hire the rest of the roster yet. One clean hire teaches you more than five overlapping personalities.

When the folder is real, write down what you will never again accept as a result: a transcript, a vibe, a “let me know if you want me to continue.” GPT-6 Astra can talk forever. Your agent should stop.
Step 2 · Write the charter, then leave it alone
A charter is the employment contract. A daily brief is today’s assignment. Most people smash them into one blob and then wonder why the agent gets dumber every morning.
Write the charter once, as a file the runtime loads every run. The charter does not change because you slept badly. The brief does.
Stop editing the contract for sport.
Five fields. Outcome. Sources. Constraints. Deliverable. Review point.
No more on the first hire. If a field is missing, you hired a chatbot with a name.
Outcome. The change in the world when the job is finished. Not the activity. “The partner pack for this week exists and is ready for my review” is an outcome. “Look through email” is a hobby.
Sources. Where the agent is allowed to look. Inbox labels. A drive folder. A CRM view. A URL list. If it is not on this list, the agent does not go hunting through your whole life.
Constraints. Timebox, tone, language, what to skip. “Do not open personal mail.” “Stop after 40 minutes.” “Draft in English.” “If a source is missing, log the gap. Do not invent the missing file.”
Deliverable. The exact artifacts and where they go. Path, filename pattern, format. “ops/YYYY-MM-DD/brief.md, form-draft.pdf, action-log.md.” If you cannot point at it, it is not a deliverable.
Review point. Where a human is still in the loop. “I read the brief before anything leaves the machine.” “I submit the form.” “I send the chases.” The review point is a door, not a vibe.
Here is Owen’s charter in the same five fields, filled in so you can steal the skeleton, not the business.
Outcome: a review-ready weekly residue pack exists by Sunday night.
Sources: the partners@ inbox, the /partners/forms folder, the chase list in ops/people.md.
Constraints: no personal mail, no sending, no submitting, no deleting. Forty-minute cap. Log gaps instead of guessing.
Deliverable: dated folder with brief, unsubmitted form draft, action log.
Review point: you open the folder Monday morning before any outbound action.
That charter should survive a month. What changes day to day is the brief: “This week the form has a new field for headcount. The chase list added Mira. Ignore the bounce from last Thursday.”
If you rewrite the charter because Mira appeared, you do not have a company. You have a mood.
Then the fences. A fence is a verb the agent may not finish without approval. Put them in a list the runtime can actually enforce, not in a paragraph the model can “interpret.”
Send. No mail, no DM, no comment on a ticket, no “quick ping” from the agent’s own address.
Spend. No checkout, no invoice pay, no upgrade, no adding a seat.
Publish. No post, no go-live, no customer-facing page, no “just update the bio.”
Delete. No trash, no archive-as-delete, no overwrite of the only copy.
Legal. No contract accept, no signature, no policy change, no sending anything that looks like advice you would want a lawyer to see.
Send. Spend. Publish. Delete. Legal. Five verbs GPT-6 Astra does not finish without you.
Everything in that list routes to an approval desk: a pending folder, a queue, or a message that includes the artifact and waits. The employee prepares. You permit.
People skip fences to keep the lid shut. That is how a polite agent mails the wrong thread or publishes a name you were not ready to share.
GPT-6 Astra is strong enough to take those actions if you hand it the tools. Strength is not permission.
The engine proposes. The fence decides.
When the agent fails, first ask whether the brief was bad, the sources moved, or a fence was missing. Only then touch the contract.
Step 3 · Give tools and logins once
An employee with no tools is a narrator. An employee with your whole machine and no map is a hazard.
GPT-6 Astra in a chat box is still you, typing. You want the middle: a shared environment, granted once, boring on purpose.
Your homemade agents should live in one place. A folder on a laptop is enough for the first hire.

A VPS is better when you want the roster to work while the lid is shut for real. A cloud computer is useful when the job needs a persistent desktop, a real browser profile, and files that do not vanish when a tab dies.
Pick one. Do not split the company across five vendor chat boxes.
Five chat windows is not a company. It is five tabs with a shared folder.
The environment is the office. GPT-6 Astra is the brain you put in every desk.
Give the office a small, explicit toolkit.
Files. The workspace, the memory folder, the deliverable paths. Read and write here. Not across the whole disk.
Browser. For the sites in the charter’s source list. Logged-in sessions you created. No surprise domains.
Mailbox. One working inbox the agents are allowed to read. Drafts land in a drafts folder. Sending stays fenced.
APIs. CRM, storage, issue tracker, whatever the job already uses. Keys live in the runtime environment, not in the agent’s memory notes.
Logins happen once, by you. Sign into the browser profile, drop keys into the secret store, confirm the mailbox. After that, agents reuse the office.
There is a short list of things that still need a human in the room. Write it down so the roster does not pretend otherwise.
Passwords you will not store in an agent file.
2FA prompts and hardware keys.
Captchas and “prove you are human” walls.
Payments, even small ones.
Sites that are legally or contractually human-only: banking, admin consoles, anything where a bot ToS is not a debate you want to have.

When the agent hits that list, it stops and writes the blocker into the action log. “Need you for 2FA on the partner portal.” That is a good employee. A workaround around your bank is not ambitious. It is off the charter.
They share the office and the toolbelt. They do not share a personality. Each agent gets its own role file and memory folder.
Do the office once. A sloppy setup shows up later as five half-broken logins and a founder typing passwords for a living.
Then rerun Step 1. Same Owen, same pack, now able to see the inbox without you pasting screenshots. The lid test should feel quieter.
Step 4 · Put GPT-6 Astra behind every agent
This is the center of the playbook.
Every homemade agent in the roster thinks with one engine: GPT-6 Astra. Not a mix of “this one for writing, that one for browsing, a third one because a blog said so.” One brain. Many employees.
You hire for ownership. You do not hire for model shopping.
The role is Mara or Cole or Rina. The mind they borrow is GPT-6 Astra.
Why Astra for this work, without a fake scoreboard.
Agent work is long-horizon. The job is not a clever paragraph. It is stay on the pack, keep the sources straight, write the artifacts, stop at the fence.
GPT-6 Astra was built as a computer-using model: a shift on the machine, not a ping-pong chat. Public demos have been about doing the thing, not decorating a transcript.
Quality matters more than first-token speed. A fast wrong brief makes you the cleanup crew. Astra’s value on a roster is artifacts you can skim and sign, not first drafts you have to reteach.
Long-horizon plus that quality is the whole argument. You are trying to shut the lid.
Attach the engine in a runtime you own. Keep it dull and centralized.
One model config for the whole company: model name GPT-6 Astra.
One API key, stored in the runtime environment, never in memory/ and never in a charter.
One endpoint: the official API, or a gateway you run, pointed at the same place for every agent.
Every role file inherits that config. Mara does not get a private model field. Cole does not “experiment” on Thursday.
If the runtime wants a base URL or a reasoning setting, set it once at company level. Drift is how a roster becomes five products that share a folder.
Two shared shelves around that config.
Skills library. A folder of small, reusable how-tos the employees can load: how we name files, how we write a chase note, how we fill this partner form.
A skill is not a person. It is a toolbelt item.
Any agent may use it. No agent is named after it.

Memory folder. Two layers. memory/shared for facts the whole company must not forget: the partner’s real name, the form URL, the definition of a qualified lead. memory/<agent> for the employee’s own notes: what Owen tried last week, which sender always bounces, which field on the form is new.
Memory is files. If it is only in a chat, it dies when the session dies. GPT-6 Astra can remember inside a long run. Your company needs memory that survives the run.
Cost and control, with no invented prices.
One engine is legible: one bill, one key to revoke, one rate limit.
Five models feel like sophistication until you cannot say which employee looped a browser all night. Five models is not a roster. It is a zoo.
Long jobs cost more than short ones, so put a cap in the charter and a kill switch in the runtime. If an agent hits the cap, it writes “stopped, unfinished” into the log.
Tokens are not the report. The dated folder is. If the folder is thin and usage is fat, fix the charter before you throw more engine at it.
One short aside, then we drop it. You may later park a tiny classifier in front of a skill: spam or not, invoice or not. That is plumbing, not a second brain. The roster still thinks in GPT-6 Astra.
GPT-6 Astra does the thinking. The homemade agents do the jobs. They share an office, a skill shelf, a memory wing, and one engine.
Step 5 · Hire the rest by what they own
Do not hire by personality. Hire by a patch of the company that can have a single owner.
If a job recurs every week, it is an agent. If it happens once, it is a skill. That line keeps the roster from turning into a costume party.
Five employees cover most of a small operation. Steal the names or change the nouns. Do not change the idea: each one owns an outcome.
Mara · leads
Owns: the inbound lead list, kept honest.
Outcome: every new name this week is either qualified, rejected with a reason, or waiting on a missing fact.
Definition of done: leads/YYYY-MM-DD.csv plus a short exceptions note.
Fence: she does not email the lead. She does not mark a deal won.
Cole · outreach
Owns: the chase and the first touch, in draft.
Outcome: every person who needs a nudge has a ready message sitting in drafts, matched to Mara’s list or Owen’s log.
Definition of done: draft messages in the mailbox drafts folder, plus a send queue for you.
Fence: send.
Rina · assets
Owns: the files other people are waiting on.
Outcome: the deck, the screenshot, the export, the cropped image, the pack the form asked for.
Definition of done: assets in assets/YYYY-MM-DD/ with names a stranger can read.
Fence: publish. She does not ship a customer-facing page or a public post.
Vince · inbox
Owns: what arrives.
Outcome: the working inbox is sorted into the source paths the rest of the roster is allowed to see. Personal mail untouched. Noise logged, not forwarded as work.
Definition of done: labels or folders applied, a daily inbound brief, a list of items that need a human.
Fence: send, delete. He files. He does not tidy by destroying.
Owen · weekly ops
Owns: the residue pack you already met.
Outcome: the week has a single folder that a manager can open and understand.
Definition of done: brief, form draft, action log, links to what Mara, Cole, and Rina already finished.
Fence: send, spend, publish, delete, legal. Owen is a packer, not a signer.
Each hire gets a card in the role file. Four lines. If you cannot fill it, you have a nickname, not a hire.
A nickname is not a hire. A card is.
Name.
Owns.
Definition of done.
Fence.
Name: Cole. Owns: outreach drafts for the current chase list. Definition of done: one draft per person, in drafts, with Mara’s or Owen’s source line at the top. Fence: send.
Start with the mess you actually have. Vince if it is arrival. Mara if it is a pile of names. Rina if files are missing. Cole if sentences sit unsent.
You already have a thin Owen from Step 1. Promote him with the real charter, then add the others only when you can point at work he is dropping.
Do not hire “Strategy.” That is your job.
Do not hire “Researcher” or “Writer” as people if Mara only needs skills/qualify-lead.md. A skill is a file any agent may load. Recurring ownership is the only reason to add a name.
When two agents would write the same file, kill one name. The company should be readable on a whiteboard: five boxes, five outcomes, five fences.
Run a week in miniature by hand. Vince files. Mara marks names. Rina drops assets. Cole drafts. Owen binds.
You still press every fenced verb. They are employees. They do not yet have a hallway.
Step 6 · Make agents hand work to each other
A roster without handoffs is five internships that all report to you. You become the hallway. The lid never quite shuts.

A handoff is a file, not a vibe. It has a sender, a receiver, a payload, and a definition of done for the next stage. If the next agent has to reconstruct intent from a chat, you did not hand it off. You abandoned it.
Give the company one group goal for a workflow. Example: “By Monday 9:00, the weekly partner pack is review-ready, including qualified new names, drafted chases, and the assets the form requires.”
Then give each stage a single owner.
Arrive: Vince.
Name the work: Mara.
Make the files: Rina.
Draft the humans: Cole.
Bind the week: Owen.
Vince may not “also just qualify a lead.” Mara may not “also just write the email.” Overlap is how artifacts fork.
A role description is the hallway map, not poetry.
Include, in this order:
What I own.
What I receive, from whom, in what path.
What I emit, to whom, in what path.
What I never do (the fence, plus the neighbor’s job).
What I do when the payload is incomplete.
Cole’s map, as a picture of the format:

Receives leads/YYYY-MM-DD.csv from Mara and ops/YYYY-MM-DD/action-log.md from Owen. Emits drafts into the mailbox drafts folder and a send-queue.md for the human. Never sends. Never invents a lead that Mara rejected. If a row has no source line, he logs a gap and skips that row.
The incomplete case saves you. Helpful without a payload is fiction.
GPT-6 Astra will fill a hole if you let it. The role file should leave the hole visible.
Handoffs need a tiny ticket shape, same fields every time.
Workflow name.
Stage.
Owner.
Payload path.
Group goal.
Blockers.
Next owner.
Owen can generate those tickets as part of the pack. He binds. He does not do Mara’s qualifying because a ticket looked lonely.
Group goal stays in memory/shared. Stage ownership stays in the role files. If you keep rewriting who owns the stage, you have a group chat.
Do not hire a manager agent yet. Owen binding the week is enough. A coordinator who only restates the files is extra cost.
Run the chain once in the open. Two agents on one artifact: cut a name. Two owners on one stage: pick one. A handoff that exists only in prose: make a path.
When one pack appears without you carrying folders, the hallway works. GPT-6 Astra is still one engine. The employees are finally a team.
Step 7 · Put the roster on a schedule
A team that only runs when you type “go” is still a chat. The last hire is time.
If it only runs when you type go, you did not hire anyone. You opened a tab.
GPT-6 Astra was ready. The calendar was not.

Do not schedule a workflow you have not dry-run. A dry-run is the full chain, on real sources, with fences up, while you are available to catch a stupid first version. You are not looking for perfection. You are looking for a pack you would accept as a draft.

Save the workflow only after the dry-run leaves a folder you understand. Saving means the role files, charters, fences, handoff paths, the GPT-6 Astra config, and the skills the chain loaded. That bundle should be copyable to a VPS without folklore in your head.
Then attach time. Cron is enough.
Monday 06:00 Vince sorts inbound. 06:30 Mara qualifies. 07:00 Rina pulls assets. 07:30 Cole drafts. 08:00 Owen binds. 08:10 you get one message: path to the pack, plus the approval list.
You still send, spend, publish, delete, and sign.
A laptop schedule only fires when the machine is awake. A VPS or a cloud computer makes “shut the lid” literal. Same agents. Same engine. Different building.

Put caps on the schedule the way you put fences on verbs. Max runtime, browser minutes, retries. If Owen is still packing at 10:00, the job failed in public. A quiet all-day loop is how you learn about cost the ugly way.
Once a week, open the packs. Did this artifact change a decision, or did you only admire it? If you admired it, it is a newsletter to yourself.
Delete one useless job every week. Not pause. Delete.
The skill can stay on the shelf. The schedule line goes. GPT-6 Astra will keep producing a handsome brief forever if you keep paying it to.

Use the same review to promote. If Cole’s drafts are clean for two weeks, you may move “send” to a narrow allow-list: this template, these people, this hour, still logged. Promotion is earned by artifacts, not by tenure.

When a job fails, read the action log before you touch the charter. Most failures are a moved source, a 2FA wall, or an empty handoff. Model-shopping is almost never the fix. The engine is already GPT-6 Astra. Change the employee’s map.
After a month you should have fewer scheduled jobs, and the ones that remain should be boring. Boring is the product.
GPT-6 Astra is the brain. The roster is the company.
You do not need a vendor bot with a mascot. You need an engine, a handful of homemade employees, an office they share, and a calendar that does not wait for you to sit down.
Laptop, VPS, or cloud computer. Same playbook.
The to-do list will still tell the truth. Some of the movement now happens while the lid is shut.
The fenced verbs stay yours. The review point stays yours. The weekly firing of a useless job stays yours.
Tonight, hire the first agent. One name. One folder. One definition of done on disk. Point it at GPT-6 Astra.
Give it a boring job. Shut the lid. Open the folder.
If the artifacts are there, you have an employee. If they are not, you still have a conversation, and you know what to fix.
The rest of the roster can wait until the first hire survives the lid, the stranger, and the repeat.
